title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
author: Leo Tolstoy
image: Death of Ivan Ilych Main Cover.png
summary: A judge dies at forty-five, and his colleagues think about promotions. Tolstoy’s short novel of 1886 goes back over Ivan Ilych’s correct, comfortable life and follows him through the illness that exposes it, in the translation by Louise and Aylmer Maude.

sections.heading: A judge’s life and death
paragraphs: The story opens with the news. In a break during a trial, Ivan Ilych Golovin’s colleagues read that he has died, and each thinks first of the promotions his death will bring. At the funeral his old friend Peter Ivanovich struggles with a springy pouffe while the widow asks how to get more money from the government, and then he goes on to his game of bridge.

Tolstoy then goes back over the life. Ivan Ilych was a capable lawyer who did what people of good position did, married suitably, kept his marriage at arm’s length and furnished his house to look like everyone else’s. A knock against a window frame while he is hanging curtains brings on an illness his doctors cannot name. His family pretend he is only ill; the peasant servant Gerasim alone tells him the truth and nurses him. In his last days he asks whether his whole life has been wrong, and two hours before he dies he finds light where he expected death.

sections.heading: How Tolstoy wrote it
paragraphs: Tolstoy had the story in mind from 1881, when Ivan Ilyich Mechnikov, a judicial official in Tula and brother of the biologist Ilya Mechnikov, died at forty-five. Accounts of what he said on his deathbed about the emptiness of his life reached Tolstoy through his sister-in-law Tatyana Kuzminskaya. In April 1884 Tolstoy noted in his diary that he wanted to begin something new, perhaps the death of a judge. He started it as Ivan Ilych’s own diary, changed to the third person in the autumn of 1885, and dated the finished manuscript 25 March 1886.

It was his first substantial fiction since Anna Karenina. In the years between he had gone through the crisis described in A Confession and written little except religious and moral works, and Aylmer Maude later recalled critics greeting the story as the return of the artist. It appeared in 1886 in the twelfth volume of Tolstoy’s collected Works, published by his wife Sofia Tolstaya.

sections.heading: Law, rank and medicine
paragraphs: Ivan Ilych is a product of Alexander II’s Russia. The judicial statutes of 1864 created courts independent of the administration, with public trials and juries, and the new courts needed new men; Ivan Ilych becomes one, as an examining magistrate, then a prosecutor and finally a member of the Court of Justice. Tolstoy follows his career in grades and salaries: the tenth rank when he leaves the School of Law, 3,500 roubles a year when he feels hard done by, and 5,000 when a change at the ministry rescues him.

His illness belongs to the medicine of the 1880s. The doctors speak of a floating kidney, chronic catarrh and the vermiform appendix, nobody names what is killing him, and readers have guessed at cancer ever since. What the story records exactly is the experience: the taste in the mouth, the pain in the side, opium and morphine, and doctors who, like the judge himself, have decided in advance which questions are relevant.

sections.heading: Gerasim and the lie
paragraphs: What torments Ivan Ilych most is the lie that he is only ill. His wife, his daughter, his colleagues and his doctors keep it up out of the same decorum he lived by, and it reduces his dying to an unpleasant incident, like someone bringing a bad smell into a drawing-room. The one person who does not lie is Gerasim, the butler’s young assistant, who carries out his master’s excretions without disgust and holds his legs on his shoulders through the night, saying that we shall all come to it.

The last chapters move from satire to something harder to name. Ivan Ilych rages at God, reviews his life and finds that everything good in it lies in childhood. When he admits that his life was not the right thing, and feels sorry for his son and his wife, his fear leaves him. Readers disagree about the light he sees, whether it is grace, a dying man’s vision or Tolstoy’s doctrine, and the story leaves them to decide.

sections.heading: Readers
paragraphs: The first readers were overwhelmed. The critic Vladimir Stasov wrote in April 1886 that no nation anywhere had a work of such genius, and in July Tchaikovsky noted in his diary that he was more convinced than ever that Tolstoy was the greatest of writers.

Its later readers include philosophers and doctors as well as novelists. Vladimir Nabokov ranked it among Tolstoy’s most perfect works. Martin Heidegger cited it in a footnote to Being and Time (1927), in his discussion of how people treat death as something that happens to someone else, and it has long been read by students of medicine for its account of how the living fail the dying. Akira Kurosawa’s film Ikiru (1952) borrows its situation for a Tokyo official with cancer.

sections.heading: The Maudes’ translation and this edition
paragraphs: Louise and Aylmer Maude knew Tolstoy and spent decades translating him. Their version of this story appeared in the Oxford Centenary Edition of his works that they edited, in the volume Iván Ilých and Hadji Murád (1935). Their English is plain and careful, like Tolstoy’s own, and they keep the moment near the end when Ivan Ilych tries to say forgive me and it comes out as forego, their rendering of a slip between two similar Russian words.

This Astor edition prints the Maudes’ translation complete, with chapter summaries and explanatory footnotes. The supporting material covers Tolstoy, the judicial reforms of 1864, nineteenth-century medicine, the chronology of Ivan Ilych’s career, the story’s language, publication and critical reception, with character studies and a glossary.

title: White Nights
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
summary: Over four nights on a Petersburg canal embankment, a lonely young dreamer falls in love with Nastenka, who is waiting for another man. Dostoevsky published this short sentimental novel in 1848, four months before his arrest, and revised it in 1860; Constance Garnett’s translation follows the revised text.

sections.heading: Four nights and a morning
paragraphs: The narrator is twenty-six, a minor official who has lived in St Petersburg for eight years and has hardly an acquaintance. He knows the faces he passes every day and greets the houses as friends, and when the whole city leaves for its summer villas he feels deserted. Walking home late along a canal one night, he finds a girl crying at the railing, rescues her from a drunken gentleman and sees her home. Her name is Nastenka, she is seventeen, and she agrees to meet him the next night on condition that he does not fall in love with her.

On the second night he tells her what a dreamer is, and she tells him about the young lodger who promised a year ago to come back for her. The lodger has been in Petersburg for three days and has not come. The narrator takes her letter to be forwarded, waits with her through the third night, and on the fourth tells her that he loves her. She accepts him, and minutes later the lodger walks past and calls her name. The next morning a letter arrives from Nastenka, asking his forgiveness and announcing her wedding.

sections.heading: The dreamer
paragraphs: Dostoevsky had already described the Petersburg dreamer in a newspaper column, the Petersburg Chronicle, in 1847: a man who longs for real life, is too weak to reach it, and becomes a strange creature of the neuter gender. In White Nights the dreamer describes himself. On the second night he speaks of himself in the third person, because he is ashamed, and gives an account of his condition that is funny and exact: the corner he hides in like a snail, the friend who calls once and never again, the romances he lives in his head, and the anniversaries he keeps for feelings that never happened.

Dostoevsky kept returning to the type for the rest of his writing life, and the narrator of Notes from Underground, which Garnett printed in the same volume, is one of its descendants. The early dreamer has a tenderness the later ones lose. He wants nothing from Nastenka that she cannot give, and when she chooses the other man he blesses her.

sections.heading: Publication and revision
paragraphs: White Nights appeared in the December 1848 issue of the journal Otechestvennye zapiski, subtitled a sentimental novel from the reminiscences of a dreamer and dedicated to Dostoevsky’s friend the poet Aleksei Pleshcheyev. Four months later both men were arrested with other members of the Petrashevsky circle. Dostoevsky was sentenced to death, reprieved at the place of execution in December 1849, and spent the next ten years in prison and exile in Siberia.

The first reviewers liked it. In January 1849 Aleksandr Druzhinin placed it above several of Dostoevsky’s earlier stories, though he wished the dreamer had a clearer place, time and occupation. When Dostoevsky collected his early work in 1860 he revised the style and added the long list of the dreamer’s fantasies, from Hoffmann and Walter Scott to the taking of Kazan. Constance Garnett translated the revised text.

sections.heading: Petersburg in the white nights
paragraphs: The white nights are the weeks around midsummer when St Petersburg, at almost sixty degrees north, never gets properly dark. The story happens in that season, when anyone who could afford it had left for a villa on the islands or in the country, and the empty city feels to the narrator like a wilderness. Most of the action takes place on a canal embankment, which Russian commentators identify as the Catherine Canal, now the Griboyedov Canal, and on a bench near Nastenka’s side street.

Dostoevsky’s city is full of literature. Pushkin’s poems about Petersburg lie behind its canals and small wooden houses, Rossini’s Barber of Seville gives the story its love letter, and the dreamer’s reveries come from Scott, Hoffmann and the Romantic poets. Nastenka’s dry remark, that he talks as though he were reading it out of a book, is the story’s own verdict on how much of this Petersburg life is lived at second hand.

sections.heading: Readers and film-makers
paragraphs: Radical critics of the 1860s were less kind than the first reviewers. Nikolai Dobrolyubov, writing in 1861, saw the dreamer as a forerunner of the narrator of The Insulted and Injured and had no patience with lovers who run errands for their rivals. In the same year the novelist Evgenia Tur called it one of the most poetic works in Russian literature. Its brevity and warmth have made it, for many readers since, the way into Dostoevsky.

Film-makers have taken it far from Petersburg. Luchino Visconti’s Le notti bianche (1957), with Marcello Mastroianni and Maria Schell, moved it to a modern Italian port town recreated at Cinecittà and won the Silver Lion at Venice, and Robert Bresson’s Four Nights of a Dreamer (1971) set it on the banks of the Seine.

sections.heading: Constance Garnett’s translation and this edition
paragraphs: Constance Garnett (1861–1946) translated Dostoevsky’s novels and stories for Heinemann in twelve volumes between 1912 and 1920, and her versions shaped how English readers met him for most of the twentieth century. White Nights and Other Stories, published in 1918, was the tenth, and it also contains Notes from Underground. Her English is clear and a little formal, and she keeps the story’s exclamations, broken-off sentences and repeated Nastenkas.

This Astor edition prints Garnett’s translation complete, with chapter summaries and explanatory footnotes. The supporting material covers Petersburg in 1848, the phenomenon of the white nights, Dostoevsky’s literary sources, the story’s language, characters, publication and afterlife, with character studies, critical material and a glossary.

title: The Overcoat
author: Nikolai Gogol
summary: Akaki Akakievitch, a poor copying clerk in St Petersburg, goes without supper for months to pay for a new overcoat, wears it for one day and has it stolen on the way home. Gogol’s story of 1842, in Claud Field’s translation, started a whole line of Russian fiction about poor clerks.

sections.heading: The clerk and his cloak
paragraphs: Akaki Akakievitch Bashmatchkin has copied documents in a St Petersburg government office for as long as anyone can remember. He is in his fifties, a titular councillor on four hundred roubles a year, and the younger clerks drop scraps of paper on his head and tell him it is snowing. He hardly notices. Copying is the one thing he loves, and he takes documents home to copy in the evenings for pleasure.

When the winter wind finds the holes in his cloak, the tailor Petrovitch refuses to patch it again and names a price for a new one. Akaki goes without tea and supper for months, and the thought of the new cloak becomes, in the narrator’s words, a companion on his life journey. He wears it for a single day. On the way home from a party it is torn off him in an empty square, and the important official he asks for help shouts at him until he has to be dragged out of the room. Within days he is dead, and soon afterwards a ghost starts pulling the cloaks off the backs of the city’s officials.

sections.heading: How Gogol wrote it
paragraphs: Gogol knew this world from the inside. After moving to St Petersburg from Ukraine he worked as a junior clerk in two government departments between 1829 and 1831. His friend Pavel Annenkov remembered him hearing an office anecdote, probably in the mid-1830s, about a poor clerk who saved for months to buy a fine gun and lost it from his boat on his first day’s shooting. That clerk fell ill with grief, and his colleagues clubbed together to buy him another. Gogol kept the saving and the loss and left out the happy ending.

In July 1839, at the spa town of Marienbad, Gogol dictated a first draft to the historian Mikhail Pogodin under the working title A Tale of a Clerk Who Steals Overcoats. He went on revising it for the next two years, and it went into the third volume of his collected Works. That volume is dated 1842 and was printed at the end of the year, but the censor held it up and it did not go on sale until January 1843, some months after the first part of Dead Souls.

sections.heading: Rank and money
paragraphs: Peter the Great’s Table of Ranks of 1722 divided the civil service into fourteen grades, and in Gogol’s Russia an official’s grade came before his name, as the narrator says it must. A titular councillor stood in the ninth. Akaki will never rise from it, and the story measures his life in the same exact terms: four hundred roubles a year, a kopeck put aside from every rouble, a Christmas bonus of sixty-five roubles when fifty would have been good luck, and a first price from the tailor of a hundred and fifty, more than a third of his salary.

The city is part of the reckoning. The northern cold, the narrator says, is the enemy of everyone on four hundred roubles a year, and the walk to his superior’s party crosses St Petersburg’s social map from ill-lit streets to bright ones full of lacquered sleighs and bearskins. The ghost is reported near the Katinka Bridge, Field’s name for the Kalinkin Bridge over the Fontanka, and the last shadow in the story strides off towards the Obukhov Bridge further along the same river.

sections.heading: The narrator
paragraphs: Much of the story’s effect comes from the man telling it. He will not name the department in case officials take offence, forgets where the party was held, and admits that he has never inquired who inherited Akaki’s goose-quills. For most of the story he laughs at Akaki along with the office. Then, without warning, he turns solemn: a young clerk, stopped in the middle of a practical joke, hears in Akaki’s voice the words Am I not your brother? and cannot forget them for the rest of his life.

Readers have divided over that paragraph ever since. For Russian critics of the 1840s it was the heart of the story, a plea on behalf of the downtrodden clerk. In 1919 Boris Eikhenbaum argued the opposite in his essay How Gogol’s Overcoat Is Made: that the whole story is a spoken performance of jokes, digressions and changes of tone, and that the famous humane passage is one more of those changes. Both readings start from the same pages, and the ghost at the end can be made to fit either.

sections.heading: Reception
paragraphs: At first the story attracted little comment, and even Vissarion Belinsky, Gogol’s great champion among the critics, mentioned it only in passing. Its influence showed in what came next. Within a few years Russian journals were full of stories about poor officials, and in Dostoevsky’s first novel, Poor Folk (1846), the clerk Makar Devushkin reads The Overcoat and is wounded by it because he sees himself in Akaki. In 1886 the French critic Eugène-Melchior de Vogüé wrote in Le Roman russe that a Russian man of letters had told him, We have all come out of Gogol’s Overcoat. Vogüé did not name him, and the remark is often credited to Dostoevsky without evidence.

The story has been adapted many times for stage and screen. The silent film The Overcoat of 1926, made in Leningrad by Grigori Kozintsev and Leonid Trauberg from a script by Yury Tynyanov, combines it with Gogol’s Nevsky Prospect, and the animator Yuri Norstein began an animated version in 1981 that has occupied him for decades.

sections.heading: Claud Field’s translation and this edition
paragraphs: The translation is Claud Field’s, from The Mantle and Other Stories, published in London by T. Werner Laurie in 1916 with Prosper Mérimée’s essay on Gogol as a preface. Field (1863–1941) also translated al-Ghazali and Meister Eckhart, and his English is brisk and plain. He calls the garment a cloak and sometimes a mantle, gives the Kalinkin Bridge as the Katinka Bridge, and uses the title Superintendent both for the police officer Akaki visits first and for the important personage he visits second. Where Gogol’s Russian says I am your brother, Field’s young clerk hears a question.

This Astor edition prints Field’s translation complete, with 49 explanatory footnotes and five Story So Far and Context sections. Further material covers St Petersburg, the Table of Ranks, money and clothing, Gogol’s narrative style, the story’s sources, and its reception, translations and adaptations. The volume also includes critical perspectives, a glossary and teaching pathways.

title: Notes from Underground
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
summary: “I am a sick man.... I am a spiteful man.” A retired official, writing notes he says nobody will read, argues that people will always choose freedom over their own good, and then tells how at twenty-four he humiliated a young woman called Liza. Dostoevsky’s short novel of 1864, in Constance Garnett’s translation.

sections.heading: Two parts
paragraphs: The narrator is forty, a collegiate assessor who retired when a distant relation left him six thousand roubles, and he lives alone in a corner on the edge of St Petersburg. The first part, Underground, is his argument with an audience he calls gentlemen and says does not exist. Too much consciousness, he says, is a disease. The man of action accepts the stone wall of the laws of nature; the conscious man can neither accept it nor break it. And people will always prefer freedom, even the freedom to harm themselves, to any happiness worked out for them in advance.

À Propos of the Wet Snow, the second part, goes back sixteen years to the life behind the argument. At twenty-four the narrator stalks an officer who once moved him aside without noticing him, forces himself on a farewell dinner for a schoolfellow he hates, and ends the night in a brothel with Liza, a young woman from Riga. He moves her to tears with a speech about her future and gives her his address. When she comes to him a few days later he humiliates her, and she leaves without taking his money.

sections.heading: Chernyshevsky and the crystal palace
paragraphs: Dostoevsky wrote the book early in 1864, while his first wife was dying in Moscow, and it is partly an answer to Nikolai Chernyshevsky’s novel What Is to Be Done? (1863). Chernyshevsky argued that enlightened self-interest would make people good, and in his heroine’s fourth dream the rational future lives in a palace of iron and glass. Dostoevsky had seen the real Crystal Palace, the hall built for the Great Exhibition of 1851, in London in 1862, and had written about it in Winter Notes on Summer Impressions.

Nobody could put out his tongue at such a palace, the narrator says, and he will not call a hen-house a mansion just because it keeps him dry. Dostoevsky meant the argument to lead somewhere. When the first part appeared he complained to his brother that the censors had passed his mockery and blasphemy and struck out the places where he drew from it the need for faith and Christ, in the chapter he thought the most important.

sections.heading: Publication
paragraphs: Notes from Underground appeared in 1864 in Epokha, the journal Dostoevsky ran with his brother Mikhail: the first part in a double issue that came out at the end of March, the second in the April issue. Dostoevsky added a footnote to the title saying that the writer of the notes was imaginary, but that such people must exist in Russian society given the circumstances in which it had been formed.

At the time the book drew almost no response. The satirist Saltykov-Shchedrin mocked the journal and its contributors in a pamphlet, and serious critical attention came only after Crime and Punishment in 1866. Garnett’s translation keeps the book’s frame: Dostoevsky’s footnote, the lines from Nekrasov at the head of the second part, and the editor’s note at the end, which says that the paradoxalist could not stop writing but that we may stop here.

sections.heading: The narrator and his readers
paragraphs: The voice is the book. The narrator contradicts himself on purpose, confesses to lying and then to lying about the confession, and argues with objections he later admits he has invented. Dostoevsky told his brother that the first part might look like chatter, and that the chatter would be resolved in the last two chapters by an unexpected catastrophe, like a transition in music.

Readers have argued ever since about how far to trust him. He calls himself an anti-hero, and he rounds on those who judge him: he has only carried to an extreme, he says, what they have not dared to carry half-way. The one person in the book who acts freely and generously is Liza, and many readers take her refusal of his money as the book’s real answer to its first part.

sections.heading: Later readers
paragraphs: In Russia the critic Nikolai Mikhailovsky gave the book a central place in his essay A Cruel Talent (1882), an attack on what he saw as Dostoevsky’s appetite for tormenting his characters. Abroad its reputation grew through a French adaptation, L’Esprit souterrain (1886), which joined the second part to Dostoevsky’s earlier story The Landlady. Friedrich Nietzsche found it by chance in a bookshop in Nice in 1887 and wrote to a friend that he had felt an immediate kinship with its author. Twentieth-century readers made the narrator a founding figure of existentialism, and Walter Kaufmann began his anthology Existentialism from Dostoevsky to Sartre (1956) with him.

sections.heading: Constance Garnett’s translation and this edition
paragraphs: Garnett’s translation was published in 1918 in the tenth volume of her Novels of Fyodor Dostoevsky, where it follows White Nights. Her English is clear and a little stately, which suits the narrator’s mock formality; she calls the crystal palace the Palace of Crystal, and keeps his gentlemen, his dashes and his broken-off sentences.

This Astor edition prints Garnett’s translation complete, with chapter summaries and explanatory footnotes. The supporting material covers Chernyshevsky and rational egoism, the Crystal Palace, Russian society in the 1860s, the passage the censor removed, the book’s language, reception and later influence, with critical perspectives, a glossary and a publication history.
